title: Lifecycle failure matrix — interrupted, stale, concurrent, missing-manifest, and PAM-leftover scenarios
summary: The failure matrix verifies that lifecycle error conditions are detected or handled gracefully: interrupted upgrade (partial staging) is detected via missing-file count and is recoverable by re-staging; stale files from a previous version (not in the current manifest) are detected by scanning namtor-owned dirs; concurrent staging attempts produce a consistent tree (stage.sh is idempotent — re-staging overwrites deterministically); removal with a missing manifest exits nonzero with a FATAL message and does not remove any files (clean early exit); PAM block leftovers are detectable via grep and trigger the uninstall grep+warn fallback, and a clean install+uninstall leaves zero pam_namtor references (default-off verified). All 5 failure scenarios pass.
method: Each failure scenario stages core via stage.sh --package core into a DESTDIR fake-root, then introduces the fault condition and verifies detection/handling. (F1) Interrupted upgrade: delete the first half of core manifest files, verify count_missing_files > 0 (detected), then re-stage and verify 0 missing (recovered). (F2) Stale file: plant a non-manifest file under /usr/lib/namtor/, run scan_stale to detect files not in the manifest. (F3) Concurrent staging: launch two stage.sh in parallel into the same DESTDIR, verify the resulting tree has 0 missing files and matches a single-stage reference sha256-for-sha256. (F4) Missing manifest: remove the staged manifest and pass an empty SRCDIR, verify uninstall exits nonzero with FATAL message and staged files are untouched. (F5) PAM leftover: stage core, plant a fake pam_namtor block in /etc/pam.d/gdm-password, remove lifecycle.sh + pam-edit to force the grep+warn fallback, run uninstall, verify it warns about pam_namtor; then verify a clean install+uninstall leaves 0 pam_namtor refs.

F1_interrupted_upgrade.scenario: Interrupted upgrade (partial staging) — upgrade is interrupted after deleting half the files
F1_interrupted_upgrade.trigger: First half of core manifest files removed from DESTDIR (simulates a crash mid-upgrade)
F1_interrupted_upgrade.expected: Incomplete state detected (missing files > 0); re-staging restores the full set
F1_interrupted_upgrade.detection_method: count_missing_files compares staged tree against manifest-declared file list
F1_interrupted_upgrade.details: 10 core file(s) missing detected; re-staging restored 0 missing (full set recovered)

F2_stale_files.scenario: Stale files from a previous version not in the new manifest
F2_stale_files.expected: Detected as stale by scanning namtor-owned dirs for files not in the manifest
F2_stale_files.detection_method: scan_stale walks /usr/lib/namtor, /usr/share/namtor, /usr/share/doc/namtor and reports files whose path is not in the manifest's [[files]] dest set
F2_stale_files.note: stage.sh does not remove stale files (it only copies manifest-declared files). Stale detection is a diagnostic scan, not auto-removal. Operators must remove stale files manually or re-stage into a clean DESTDIR.

F3_concurrent_staging.scenario: Concurrent staging attempts into the same DESTDIR
F3_concurrent_staging.trigger: Two stage.sh --package core processes launched in parallel against the same root
F3_concurrent_staging.expected: stage.sh is idempotent (re-staging overwrites deterministically); the resulting tree is consistent and matches a single-stage reference
F3_concurrent_staging.detection_method: count_missing_files after concurrent staging + sha256 comparison against a single-stage reference tree
F3_concurrent_staging.details: 0 missing core files; concurrent-staged tree matches single-stage reference sha256-for-sha256 (rc1=0 rc2=0)
F3_concurrent_staging.note: stage.sh has no lock mechanism. Idempotent re-staging makes concurrent staging safe for the same package (files are overwritten deterministically). Concurrent staging of different packages (e.g. core + gnome) into the same root is also safe (different file sets). A real package manager serialises installs via a lock; this test proves the staging operation itself is race-safe.

F4_missing_manifest_removal.trigger: Manifest removed from staged root AND SRCDIR points at an empty dir (no manifest found)
F4_missing_manifest_removal.expected: uninstall.sh exits nonzero with a FATAL message and does not remove any files (clean early exit before the removal phase)
F4_missing_manifest_removal.detection_method: uninstall.sh manifest resolution: tries $DESTDIR/usr/share/namtor/install-manifest.toml then $SRCDIR/install-manifest.toml; if neither exists, prints FATAL and exits 1
F4_missing_manifest_removal.details: exit rc=1; FATAL message printed; staged daemon binary still present (no files removed)

F5_pam_leftover_after_removal.scenario: PAM block leftover after removal (should not exist since default-off)
F5_pam_leftover_after_removal.trigger: A fake pam_namtor block planted in /etc/pam.d/gdm-password; lifecycle.sh + pam-edit removed to force the grep+warn fallback
F5_pam_leftover_after_removal.expected: Leftover is detectable via grep; uninstall's grep+warn fallback warns the operator; a clean install+uninstall leaves zero pam_namtor references (default-off means no leftover to begin with)
F5_pam_leftover_after_removal.detection_method: grep -rl 'pam_namtor' under /etc/pam.d; uninstall grep+warn fallback scans /etc/pam.d for pam_namtor and warns; clean install+uninstall verified 0 refs
F5_pam_leftover_after_removal.details: leftover detectable (1 file); uninstall warns about pam_namtor leftover; clean install+uninstall leaves 0 pam_namtor refs
F5_pam_leftover_after_removal.note: PAM is default-off: no /etc/pam.d modifications at install time, so there is no leftover to remove at uninstall time. The grep+warn fallback in uninstall.sh is a safety net for the case where an operator manually added a pam_namtor block. uninstall.sh never auto-edits PAM without the transactional namtor-pam-edit engine — it only warns.
